newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Patten blasts China over HK's new election laws.
newsitem.headline: Patten blasts China over HK's new election laws.

text.p: Hong Kong Governor Chris Patten on Monday slammed China-inspired changes to Hong Kong's election rules as a ploy that would slash the number of democrats who can get elected.
Patten, speaking to reporters after returning from London, where he briefed new Prime Minister Tony Blair, described the plan as "extremely sad".
"(They) will be introducing a voting system for the geographical constitutencies, the purpose of which will be to reduce the number of pro-democracy candidates who can get elected," Patten said.

He also criticised the future government of post-colonial leader Tung Chee-hwa for saying it was too late to consult the general public on the proposed changes to the liberal election rules that Patten introduced after he arrived in 1992. "That's extremely sad. I can't understand why there should be no time," Patten said.

Last week the 150-strong Preparatory Committee, which is setting up Hong Kong's post-handover political structures, proposed to change the current electoral laws for the 60-seat legislature after Britain hands the territory back to China at midnight on June 30. Under the formula endorsed by China, Tung would have to choose either multi-seat, single-vote polls or proportional representation to fill the 20 directly elected seats under geographic constitutencies, which are currently returned by first-pass-the-post voting system.
Thirty seats are allocated to business and professional bodies in what are known as "functional constitutencies".
The remaining 10, another major bone of contention with the pro-democracy camp in Hong Kong, will be chosen by an 800-strong selection committee with a highly complicated makeup.
But Tung had rejected claims that the proposed election laws would dent the prospect of the pro-democracy camp. "I think they have very opportunity to participate and I hope they will," he said.
Presently, 25 of the 60 legislators are from the pro-democracy camp.
Tung also said the first election held under Chinese rule would likely be in the second quarter of 1998.
Britain's new Hong Kong minister, Derek Fatchett, said there would be no search for a "soft relationship" with China after the July 1 handover.

"There can be no washing of hands after July 1, there can be no looking for a soft relationship. We want a warm relationship with China, but it is not going to be a relationship in which we cast ourselves as subordinates looking for gifts," Fatchett told the South China Morning Post on Monday.
On Monday, human rights groups in the territory expressed concern about apparent self-censorship here by distributors of a book by China's best-known dissident, Wei Jingsheng, who is now in jail.

Fears grew after the South China Morning Post reported that Wei's book, "The Courage to Stand Alone", may have been labelled by the Penguin publishing group as too sensitive to promote the anthology of essays and letters in Hong Kong.
